LESSON OBJECTIVE
Find every real input that makes a rational expression undefined, including restrictions hidden by cancellation or division. The governing rule is denominator ≠ 0.
CORE IDEA

A rational expression is defined wherever its original denominator is nonzero. Always determine restrictions before simplifying: a canceled factor still creates an excluded input in the original expression.
KEY DEFINITIONS

Domain: all permitted inputs. Undefined value: an input that makes a denominator zero. Excluded value: a number omitted from the domain. Removable hole: an excluded input that disappears from a simplified formula.
CORE RULE
For P(x)/Q(x), solve Q(x)=0 and exclude those real roots. If dividing by a rational expression A(x)/B(x), also require A(x)≠0 because the divisor cannot equal zero.
HOW IT WORKS

1. Identify every original denominator. 2. Factor each denominator or solve its zeros. 3. If dividing, exclude zeros of the divisor itself. 4. Apply any contextual constraints. 5. State the domain before cancellation.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — LINEAR DENOMINATOR
For 1/(x−4), solve x−4=0 to get x=4. The domain is all real numbers except 4. The numerator being 1 creates no restriction.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — FACTORED QUADRATIC
For (x+3)/(x²−9), factor x²−9=(x−3)(x+3). The denominator vanishes at x=−3 and x=3. Even though x+3 cancels algebraically, both exclusions remain.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — REPEATED FACTOR
For (x²−16)/(x²−8x+16), factor the denominator as (x−4)². Only x=4 is forbidden; a repeated zero is still one distinct excluded input.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — DIVIDING RATIONAL EXPRESSIONS
For ((x−1)/(x+1)) ÷ ((x−1)/(x−3)), the denominators require x≠−1,3. The divisor (x−1)/(x−3) must also be nonzero, so x≠1. Final exclusions: −1,1,3.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5 — CONTEXT AND PARAMETERS
If R(t)=t/(t−5) models positive time t, the context requires t>0 and the denominator requires t≠5. For D(x)=x²−(k+1)x+k=(x−1)(x−k), forbidden inputs are 1 and k.
WORKED EXAMPLE 6 — NO REAL RESTRICTION
For 1/(x²+1), x²≥0 for all real x, so x²+1≥1 and never vanishes. Its real domain is all real numbers.
COMMON MISTAKES

Do not exclude zeros of a numerator unless that expression is the divisor. Do not restore a canceled denominator zero. Do not assume a quadratic always has real zeros. Check context limits separately.
EXAM STRATEGY

Find restrictions from the ORIGINAL expression before doing any algebraic cancellation. Factoring denominators is usually fastest; use the discriminant or completing the square when a quadratic does not factor over the reals.
QUICK CHECK
1) 5/(x+2) is undefined at x=−2. 2) (x²−25)/(x−5) still excludes x=5 after simplification. 3) 1/(x²+1) has no real exclusions. 4) A zero numerator alone does not make a fraction undefined.
LESSON RECAP
Denominator zeros are forbidden. Record restrictions first, factor carefully, preserve holes, and for division also exclude inputs that make the divisor zero. Apply real-world domain constraints.
